cim: Not-So-Large Language Model Fits On A Floppy Disk
kihagyva: P3: 50 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Not-So-Large Language Model Fits On A Floppy Disk
szoveg_eredeti:
At some point when hackers start pushing edge cases, nomenclature gets weird, like Large Language Models, or LLMs. At some point, the word “large” obviously becomes impossible to justify, but we’re not going to call [WollyMonjac]’s Tiny2.1 DOS PC Chatbot just a ‘language model’ — perhaps “transformer” is the better term. That’s what LLMs and not-so-L-LMs like this one are under the hood, after all.

In any case, this one was written in Turbo C 2.0 by the no-debate ‘large’ LLM Fable 5.2 and trained by Opus 5.5. So for those of you who’ve got this one on their apocalypse bingo card: yes, machines are making machines. This second-gen transformer targets a 486DX or Pentium processor and runs on DOS, and you can get it onto the machine on a single period-appropriate floppy disk.

The actual network is 380 KB of 8-bit weights, while the rest of the floppy would hold the handy interface. As you might imagine, it needs 540 KB of free memory to run in. The transformer holds 3,500 facts in its 367K-parameter but outside of that it makes stuff up with the reckless abandon that these models can’t escape, regardless of size.

The project is of course more of a conversation-starter than anything else, though if you want to train it on your own 3,500 facts the scripts for that are on GitHub under an MIT license. We’ve seen an LLM on a 486 before, but being able to easily curate exactly what the model knows raises some interesting possibilities.

There was a company that had developed one such ASIC, but AMD bought them out. Seeing as it might cannibalize the GPU market, I doubt that they’ll release it.

I don’t think a model in silicon is practical. How are you going to update it…. And AMD would not care if it canabilized the gpu market. As that share would go to this chip then.

That’s the neat part: you don’t! The model is part of the chip, that’s where efficiency comes from. Sure, you’ve got to toss your chip after the next greatest update comes around, but your old GPU might not be able to run it well either. My understanding was that this technology was being looked at for small, specific neural nets like for image recognition more than full-size LLMs, but I could see it happening if/when we hit a plateau on model complexity and the cost of missing out on the upgrade thereby becomes lower.

It seems like some part of such a chip could be built with flash or other mutable logic, and still be quite fast yet (slightly?) updateable.

I don’t think the risk of a rug-pull is too high, because we have options. Open-weight models from Chinese developers are available now and can be run by anybody with a sufficiently powerful computer cluster. The hardware requirements are out of reach for personal use, but a business with sufficient funding could do it. These models aren’t as capable as the current state of the art models, but they’re still very good.

At the lower end, there are tons of models today that you can run locally on a decent PC. They’re not in the same class as the larger cloud-based models, but are still very useful for help with software programming, data manipulation, writing or editing text, image generation, and lots of other stuff.

My understanding is that LLM ASICs are intended to be an improvement over the GPU hardware that everyone is using now, and would allow big cloud models to be built at lower cost and with lower power requirements, etc. But they are still general-purpose LLM accelerators, not an actual LLM model fixed in silicon. Fixing an entire state-of-the art model into the silicon of a single chip would be physically and economically unfeasible, I believe, and it would also mean you could never change or upgrade the model or its architecture. It would quickly become obsolete.
